title: Excel Functions vs Formulas
description: Excel functions vs formulas: learn the difference. A formula is the calculation you write; a function is a built-in tool like SUM, AVERAGE or IF that powers it.
intro: Excel functions vs formulas is the distinction that trips up most beginners, yet the two words are not opposites. A formula is any instruction you type that starts with = and produces a result; a function is a built-in, pre-named operation such as SUM, AVERAGE or IF that you call from inside a formula. This guide separates the two clearly, shows the same calculation written both ways, and explains where functions become unavoidable.
prerequisites: Excel or Google Sheets open in front of you

sections.title: A Formula Is the Instruction, a Function Is the Tool
sections.content: A formula is any expression that begins with = and returns a value. A function is a built-in, named routine - SUM, AVERAGE, IF and several hundred others - that you call inside a formula. Every function needs a formula to live in, but a formula does not need a function. The hierarchy is one-way: functions are a subset of formulas, never the other way round.

example.result: Adds the three cells with plain arithmetic - a formula containing no function at all
example.explanation: The + operator does all the work here, so Excel never calls a built-in function. This is still a formula: it starts with = and calculates something.

tips: If a cell entry starts with = it is a formula; if it starts with a letter, digit or apostrophe it is a value or text.

sections.title: The Same Result, Written Two Ways
sections.content: Most everyday calculations can be expressed either as manual arithmetic or as a function call. Adding five cells with + signs and wrapping them in SUM describe exactly the same operation - the function version is simply shorter to type, easier to extend when rows are inserted, and far less likely to contain a typo.

example.explanation: =A1+A2+A3+A4+A5 also returns 150. The function version scales: changing the range to A1:A500 is a two-character edit, while the manual version would need 496 more terms.

tips: SUM ignores text and blank cells inside the range, so a stray column header or empty cell will not break the total.

sections.title: Functions Hide Logic That Is Painful to Write by Hand
sections.content: Some functions do work you can technically express with operators but would never want to. AVERAGE is the classic case: the manual equivalent has to sum a range and divide by a count, and it has to decide which cells deserve to be counted in the first place.

example.explanation: =SUM(A1:A5)/COUNT(A1:A5) produces the same 30, but AVERAGE skips blanks and text automatically, so you never have to think about which cells COUNT would have included.

tips: COUNT counts numeric cells only; COUNTA counts every non-empty cell. AVERAGE follows COUNT's behaviour.

sections.title: Where Functions Become Unavoidable
sections.content: Conditional logic is the point where plain arithmetic runs out entirely. IF evaluates a test that resolves to TRUE or FALSE, then returns one result or another. There is no combination of +, - and * that can branch like that, which is why IF is the gateway function to everything more advanced.

example.result: Returns Pass when C2 is 60 or greater, otherwise Fail
example.explanation: IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false) is a formula whose entire behaviour comes from the function call - strip the IF away and nothing useful remains.

tips: Text results must be wrapped in double quotes; numbers and cell references are written bare.

sections.title: Excel and Google Sheets: One Small Difference
sections.content: The formula-versus-function model is identical in both apps, and SUM, AVERAGE and IF return the same answers in both. What changes are the edges: Excel adds structured table references and LAMBDA, while Google Sheets leans on ARRAYFORMULA and its own extras such as QUERY and IMPORTRANGE.

example.result: Totals the Price column of the Excel table named Products, wherever that table sits in the workbook
example.explanation: Google Sheets has no structured references, so the Sheets equivalent is =SUM(Products!C2:C100) - the same total, written with an explicit range instead of a table column name.

tips: Functions are conventionally written in uppercase; both apps accept lowercase and normalise it for you.

functionsUsed.name: SUM
functionsUsed.description: SUM adds all the numbers in a range of cells and returns the total.

functionsUsed.name: AVERAGE
functionsUsed.description: AVERAGE returns the arithmetic mean of a set of numbers.

functionsUsed.name: IF
functionsUsed.description: IF performs a logical test and returns one value if true and another if false.

summary: A formula is any = expression that calculates a result, while a function is a built-in named operation you call from inside that formula. Every function is used in a formula, but plenty of formulas use no function at all - =A1+A2+A3 proves it. Practically, functions win wherever logic gets complex: SUM and AVERAGE replace long chains of arithmetic, and IF introduces branching that operators alone cannot express.
